sweep_summary: All three sweep items are one work: Alderete & Bob, 'A corpus-based approach to Tahltan stress' — the Glottolog text entry, its Benjamins DOI record (Crossref: Athabaskan Prosody, pp. 369-391, issued 2005-10-26), and the ANLA archive copy CN002AB2002 of the February-2002 manuscript. The ANLA record (fetched sources via the archive's Drupal API; Glottolog's item.xml URL is dead) describes it as 'ca. 26 (2 per page)', which matches the held author-site preprint ('Version: February 2002', 27 ms pages 2-up). That preprint is the catalog's deciding source, already on file and now copied into the audit folder; re-read, it confirms the MORPHOLOGICAL coding (stem syllable always stressed, absolute in nouns, obligatory pre-stem stress, alternating secondaries; main stress last in 85%). No new Tahltan stress literature surfaced: Crossref bibliographic search for 'Tahltan stress' returns only A&B 2005 and Cook 1972; archive.org has nothing; Semantic Scholar rate-limited; Two corrections for the audit store's wishlist: Cook 1972 is doi:10.1086/465221 (not 465223 = Walker, Zuni) and Nater 1989 is doi:10.1086/466103 (not 466102 = Thompson, Koyukon); both remain paywalled (uchicago 403). Held Alderete & Blenkiron 2014 synopsis sec. 2.3 and Nater 2006 (stem stress in finite verbs unless a stress-attracting prefix overrides) agree with and refine the coding. Bob 1999 UBC thesis still unreachable (UBC bot-block). Suggested action: none for the coding; fix the two DOIs and the dead ANLA URL in the per-language bibliography.

new_statements.quote: In general, we have found that there is a strong correlation between stem position and primary stress, which is consistent with Cook's findings. Furthermore, the only exceptions to this generalization are in verbs, which is also true of Nater's exceptions to the stress-to-stem generalization. Concerning stress and rhythm, our results compare to Cook's in that stress is, by and large, rhythmically distributed in the sense that two adjacent syllables of equal stress rank are strongly avoided. However, as shown in 3.3 and 3.4, there are certain important contexts where stress clash is permitted

new_statements.reading: Primary stress falls on the (morphological) stem syllable — absolute in nouns, with a small verb-only residue — and secondary stresses alternate leftward from it with an obligatory pre-stem stress; syllable weight plays only a marginal role (CVV may attract stress off the stem). The authors explicitly reconcile Cook 1972 (stem + alternating rule) and Nater 1989 (phonemic, non-iterative stress) in favour of a morphologically anchored, rhythmically distributed system. This is the catalog's own deciding source read again in full; the passage quoted here is its summary section, which complements the sec. 3.1 generalizations already in the record.

audit.reasoning: The record rests on the dedicated, most recent and most extensive study of Tahltan stress (Alderete & Bob 2005, corpus of 370 tallied words), held as the author-site preprint with a clean column-split text; every fragment of the deciding quotation, the domain quote and the exceptions quote is verbatim at the stated ms pages (6, 8, 11, 13, 14). The held Alderete & Blenkiron 2014 synopsis agrees. The annotated Tahltan bibliography (fetched sources now) and Alderete 2005 (fetched sources now) both confirm that the stress literature consists of Cook 1972, Nater 1989 and A&B, with A&B reconciling the other two; The MORPHOLOGICAL coding (stem syllable stressed, absolute in nouns, ~88% in 4-syllable words; main stress = last stress in 85%) matches the source

sources.citation: Alderete, John & Amber Blenkiron. 2014. Tahltan grammar synopsis. Ms., Simon Fraser University. (held secondary; not in the sweep list)
sources.quote: Main stress rule: assign main stress to the stem syllable (generally final syllable, but exceptionally the penult) and secondary stress to alternating syllables counting backwards from the main stress. Additionally, there must be a stress on a pre-stem syllable, which can lead to two adjacent stressed syllables if there is only one pre-stem syllable.
sources.locator: sec. 2.3 Suprasegmentals, (14) Stress assignment rule, ms pp. 7-8
sources.note: Fieldworker's own grammar synopsis restating A&B 2005 as a rule: main stress on the stem, alternating secondaries leftward, obligatory pre-stem stress; phonetic correlates higher F0, loudness, duration. Agrees with the catalog's MORPHOLOGICAL coding.

sources.citation: Nater, Hank F. 2006. Athabascan verb stem structure: Tahltan. In G. Rowicka & E. Carlin (eds.), What's in a verb?, 53-72. Utrecht: LOT. (held, open access; not in the sweep list)
sources.quote: In finite verbs not containing a stress-attracting prefix (cf. fn. 3 and 16), the stem receives the stress. [...] Where two stress-attracting non-pronominal prefixes occur in sequence, location of stress is determined by the leftmost such prefix.
sources.note: Nater's later (Iskut-based) statement: stem stress is the default in finite verbs, overridden by lexically 'stress-attracting' prefixes, the leftmost winning when two co-occur. This is the same verb-only exception class A&B report (chart (7): 7/50 verbs without primary stem stress) and refines the catalog's exceptions note with a morphological mechanism; it does not change the coding.

Hardwick 1984)'; 'Under stress, Fo may rise and fall as a function of stress in unmarked syllables' vs low level Fo in low-marked stressed syllables. No independent stress-placement rule; supports the record's tone_note that stress is described independently of the vestigial low-marked tone.
